Eggs of Eulamprus quoyii deposited in nests maintained at a constant incubation temperature of 25.8 °C [T = 25.8 °C] exhibit a developmental period of approximately 71 days [ab = approximately 71 days], a duration comparable to that of other large scincid lizards from temperate Australia. Hatchlings emerging from these eggs display a snout-to-vent length at birth of 3.845 cm [Lb = 3.845 cm] and a wet weight at birth of 0.97 grams [Wwb = 0.97 grams]. This modest neonatal mass, less than one gram, reflects the relatively small yolk reserves allocated to each offspring in this viviparous species, a trait that is balanced by the production of multiple offspring per clutch. The embryos rely entirely on yolk nutrients throughout gestation, and the success of the eggs at this thermal regime underscores the sensitivity of incubation duration to slight variations in nest temperature. Field studies have noted that the precise timing of hatching can shift by several days in response to minor thermal fluctuations, but the 71-day benchmark provides a reliable baseline for captive-rearing protocols.

As juveniles grow and approach reproductive maturation, they undergo a pronounced increase in both length and mass. The snout-to-vent length at puberty is reached at approximately 9 cm [Lp = approximately 9 cm], a threshold that corresponds with the onset of gonadal activity and the first detectable levels of circulating sex hormones. At this stage, individuals typically attain a wet weight at puberty of about 11 grams [Wwp = about 11 grams], representing a more than tenfold increase over their birth mass. This period of rapid somatic growth is critical for building the structural and energetic reserves necessary for successful reproduction. The transition from juvenile to sub-adult is marked by a distinct acceleration in growth rate, after which the body mass gain begins to decelerate as the lizard channels more resources toward reproductive development. The attainment of the 9 cm SVL benchmark is considered a reliable indicator of approaching first reproduction in this species.

The maximum snout-to-vent length for this species has been recorded at 13 cm [Li = 13 cm], a value based on unpublished observations by Schwarzkopf, representing the ultimate size achievable by the most long-lived individuals. Corresponding to this ultimate length, the ultimate wet weight recorded in the same unpublished dataset is 41.8 g [Wwi = 41.8 g]rams, a mass that reflects a substantial accumulation of body tissue and stored energy reserves over a prolonged growth period. Such large individuals are typically the dominant breeders in the population, often possessing a competitive advantage in territory acquisition and mate guarding. The attainment of these upper limits of body size appears to be highly sensitive to thermal conditions during development. Under a constant thermal regime of 17.7 °C [T = 17.7 °C], growth rates are markedly slower, and it is under these cooler conditions that the species demonstrates its full longevity. The oldest documented individuals, also from Schwarzkopf's unpublished work, achieve a lifespan of 12 years [am = 12 years], a notable age for a skink of this body size at a temperature of 17.7 °C [T = 17.7 °C].

Reproductive output in Eulamprus quoyii is strongly modulated by environmental temperature, with a clear upper bound on the rate of offspring production. When activity occurs under a mean thermal regime of 17.7 °C [T = 17.7 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is expressed as two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year], with each clutch typically containing a fixed number of offspring. The total number of offspring produced across a single reproductive event averages approximately 2.5 young per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 2.5 young per clutch], a relatively modest litter size characteristic of many viviparous temperate skinks. This combination yields an annual output of roughly 5 young per year, a rate that reflects the energetic constraints imposed by the cooler thermal environment. Warmer conditions would theoretically permit a faster pace, but the 17.7 °C benchmark corresponds to the average temperatures experienced during the active season at the core of the species' range. Under the warmer developmental conditions that characterize early clutches (25.8 °C [T = 25.8 °C]), the first successful breeding event typically occurs at an age of 375.5 days after hatching [tR = 375.5 days after hatching].

The ecological role of Eulamprus quoyii within its riparian and swampy habitats is that of an opportunistic forager, preying on a variety of invertebrates and occasionally small vertebrates. The species is diurnal and heavily reliant on basking to maintain its body temperature within an optimal metabolic range. While the asymptotic body size of 13 cm SVL is documented, some older gravid females may approach this upper limit, and their large body size facilitates the production of relatively larger offspring, enhancing juvenile survival. The wet weight at birth, less than one gram, underscores the relatively altricial state of the neonates, which must begin foraging immediately upon emergence. The species shows a strong fidelity to its home range, with individuals often recaptured within a few meters of their initial capture site over multiple years, contributing to the observed maximum lifespan of 12 years [am = 12 years] at a temperature of 17.7 °C [T = 17.7 °C]. This longevity, combined with a life history that includes relatively late first reproduction at 375.5 days after hatching, places this skink among the slower-paced members of the temperate Australian herpetofauna. The interplay between the constant incubation temperature of 25.8 °C and the reproductive development benchmarks highlights the tight coupling between thermal physiology and life history scheduling in this resilient skink.
